# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, affecting more than 64 million individuals worldwide and accounting for substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure [1]. Despite advances in pharmacological therapy and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), a large proportion of patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) remain symptomatic [2]. Importantly, the majority of HFrEF patients have a narrow QRS complex and are therefore ineligible for CRT [3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as a device-based therapy designed to improve contractile function and symptoms in this population [4].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM therapy delivers non-excitatory electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [5]. Because these high-voltage signals (approximately 7.5 V) are timed after local depolarization, they do not initiate a new action potential but instead modulate myocardial contractility [6]. Experimental studies have demonstrated that CCM enhances calcium handling by increasing phosphorylation of phospholamban and improving sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium uptake [7]. Additionally, CCM appears to reverse the fetal gene program associated with maladaptive remodeling, normalizing expression of genes governing calcium cycling and contractile proteins [8]. Such molecular changes translate into improved contractile performance without a measurable increase in myocardial oxygen consumption [9].

## Clinical Evidence

The clinical development of CCM has progressed through several randomized controlled trials. The FIX-HF-4 study was an early crossover trial demonstrating improvements in peak oxygen consumption (VO2) and quality of life with active therapy [10]. The FIX-HF-5 trial enrolled patients with NYHA class III–IV symptoms and ejection fraction ≤35% and, while not meeting its primary endpoint across the entire cohort, identified a subgroup with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% who derived significant benefit [11]. This finding informed the design of subsequent studies [12].

The pivotal FIX-HF-5C trial confirmed the benefit of CCM in patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45%, demonstrating significant improvements in peak VO2, six-minute walk distance, and quality of life as measured by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire [13]. A pooled analysis of randomized trial data further supported reductions in HF hospitalizations [14]. On the basis of these results, the Optimizer Smart device received U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval in 2019 [15].

Registry and real-world data have largely corroborated trial findings. The CCM-REG registry reported sustained improvements in NYHA functional class and quality of life over long-term follow-up, with reductions in HF hospitalization rates compared with the year preceding implantation [16]. Several observational studies have documented improvements in echocardiographic parameters, including left ventricular ejection fraction and reverse remodeling [17,18]. Additional analyses suggest a possible favorable effect on survival when observed outcomes are compared with predicted mortality from validated risk scores such as the Seattle Heart Failure Model [19].

## Safety and Patient Selection

CCM has demonstrated an acceptable safety profile across studies, with complication rates comparable to those of other implantable cardiac devices [20]. Lead dislodgement and procedure-related events are the most commonly reported complications [21]. Importantly, CCM does not appear to be proarrhythmic, and the non-excitatory signal does not interfere with concurrent implantable cardioverter-defibrillator function in most patients [22]. Current candidates are typically patients with symptomatic HFrEF, ejection fraction between 25% and 45%, narrow QRS, and persistent symptoms despite guideline-directed medical therapy [23]. The therapy is delivered by a battery-powered implantable pulse generator that is periodically recharged externally [24].

## Emerging Directions

Ongoing research is exploring CCM applications beyond classic HFrEF. Preliminary data suggest potential benefit in patients with HF and preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, an area of substantial unmet need [25,26]. The AIM HIGHer trial is evaluating CCM in patients with higher ejection fractions [27]. Investigators are also studying combined and leadless device configurations to simplify implantation and broaden eligibility [28]. Furthermore, integration of CCM with remote monitoring may enhance HF management and early detection of decompensation [29]. Cost-effectiveness analyses have begun to address the economic implications of incorporating CCM into HF care pathways [30].

## Conclusion

Cardiac contractility modulation represents a clinically meaningful addition to the device-based management of symptomatic HFrEF, particularly for patients ineligible for CRT. Robust randomized and registry data support improvements in functional capacity and quality of life, with an acceptable safety profile. Future trials clarifying effects on hard clinical endpoints and extending applicability to broader ejection fraction ranges will further define the role of this therapy.
